drills.q: Design a gate that catches an 8-point regression in a German safety slice while overall quality improves.
drills.a: Use a mandatory German safety slice threshold and max-drop rule in addition to the aggregate threshold; fail the candidate.

drills.q: Classify JSON validity, groundedness, and tone as deterministic or judge-scored.
drills.a: JSON validity is deterministic; groundedness and tone are judge-scored only if calibrated against human labels.

drills.q: Why should a 1-point drop on a 20-case slice not automatically block a release?
drills.a: The sample noise is large; 20 cases support smoke detection, not fine-grained estimates. Require more cases or a catastrophic-failure rule.

drills.q: A prompt scores 99% on the active set and 82% on held-out. Diagnose.
drills.a: Likely overfitting to the active set, though also check distribution mismatch and dataset versions.

drills.q: Write the release predicate for overall >= .90, critical slices >= .85, and no slice drop > .05.
drills.a: Pass only if every condition is true against a pinned baseline, with minimum sample counts enforced.

drills.q: A provider outage causes every case to fail. What should the gate report?
drills.a: An infrastructure/provider failure with no quality verdict, not a prompt regression; preserve the report and stop the gate.

drills.q: Design auto-revert protection against oscillation between two prompt versions.
drills.a: Pin the last accepted artifact, cap rollback attempts, do not re-gate the revert as a new candidate, and page an owner.

drills.q: When should you not build a formal prompt gate?
drills.a: For a low-stakes, single-user prompt where manual review is cheaper and no release decision depends on the result.
